article.overview: A regolith density sensor is a payload class for measuring how much mass a given volume of lunar regolith contains, usually expressed as bulk density in kilograms per cubic metre or grams per cubic centimetre, and how that density changes with depth. Bulk density matters for excavation, foundation and landing-pad engineering, and it helps interpret surface mechanical, thermal and radar measurements. No dedicated regolith density instrument has been identified in the sources reviewed as having flown on a lunar mission; a 2026 conference abstract states that no dedicated instruments have yet been flown to measure regolith physical properties on modern landing and roving missions [5]. Density information from the Apollo era came from returned core samples measured in laboratories, and from penetrometer data interpreted with those samples [2][3]. Several in-situ candidates are in development, tested in the laboratory, or have heritage on other missions, including a permittivity-based sensor proposed for China's Chang'e 8 mission [5].
article.description:
A regolith density sensor would determine the bulk density of lunar soil. Bulk density combines the mass of the solid grains with the air-free pore space between them. It depends on the grain material, the particle-size distribution, how tightly the soil has been compacted and how much of the soil volume is pore space (porosity). Because compaction and porosity change with depth, a useful measurement often needs a depth profile rather than a single value.

Several measurement principles have been proposed or tested. Core tubes and drill cores return material that can be weighed and measured in a laboratory. This is the basis of most Apollo-era density data, but it is a sampling method rather than an in-situ sensor [3]. In-situ approaches include gamma-ray attenuation or backscatter, where the detected gamma-ray spectrum depends on scattering in the surrounding material [7]; penetration resistance, from which density and porosity are inferred [2]; dielectric permittivity, which depends on the soil's electrical properties and is used to infer density [5]; and radio-frequency reflection, which has been tested in a laboratory to estimate the mass of regolith scooped by an excavator [6]. Each approach measures a different quantity or relies on an empirical calibration, so results must be interpreted together with the method that produced them.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a regolith density sensor is to provide engineering and scientific data about the surface and near-surface soil. Engineering applications include estimating how easily regolith can be excavated, how it will bear loads from landers, rovers and future surface structures, and how it will compact or deform when disturbed. The Apollo 16 penetrometer work was used to derive density, porosity and strength profiles for exactly this kind of engineering purpose [2]. Scientific applications include linking surface observations to the properties of deeper material, and providing ground truth for orbital and radar interpretations of bulk density [4]. The Chang'e 8 terrain instrument proposal explicitly targets bulk density and ice content, which indicates current interest in in-situ density measurement for both engineering and resource assessment [5].
article.operating_principle:
Different designs use different physical principles, and the operating principle of a future sensor depends on which one it adopts.

Penetration-based inference. The Apollo 16 Lunar Self-Recording Penetrometer pushed a cone into the soil and recorded the penetration force against depth on a mechanically driven drum [1]. Density and porosity are not measured directly by this method. They are derived by combining penetration resistance with surface observations and returned samples [2].

Gamma-ray densitometry. The DEN design described for the HP3 mole uses a caesium-137 gamma source and two semiconductor detectors. Density is determined at regular intervals during penetration by measuring the gamma-ray spectrum, which depends on Compton scattering in the surrounding material. The 2006 breadboard was calibrated against test materials and a Monte Carlo model [7].

Permittivity sensing. The Chang'e 8 Terrain Testing Instrument integrates a permittivity sensor with its shear vane and cone. Bulk density and ice content are inferred from the regolith's dielectric properties and relative permittivity [5].

Radio-frequency reflection. A 50 Ω open-ended microstrip line measures the phase of the reflection coefficient (S11) at 5 GHz. Regolith has a higher permittivity than air, so immersing the line shifts the reflected phase, and a linear calibration converts that shift to mass [6].

Radar-based estimation. For the Chang'e-3 landing site, bulk density was estimated from hyperbolic reflections in Lunar Penetrating Radar data. This is a remote estimate rather than an in-situ measurement [4].
article.scientific_importance: Bulk density is one of the basic physical properties needed to interpret regolith. Porosity is a dominant control on soil strength, so the same soil can behave very differently at different depths and compaction states [2]. Apollo-era density values from core tubes and penetrometer work remain important reference points [2][3]. However, Apollo sampling covered a limited number of sites, and density profiles differ between locations and between measurement methods [3][4]. A modern in-situ density sensor could provide density data at new locations and reduce reliance on remote inference [5]. The importance is therefore practical as well as scientific: without local density measurements, models of excavation and surface engineering must extrapolate from a small number of samples.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a regolith density sensor, because no flown instrument with this exact purpose has been established. The examples below are a flown penetrometer that supports density inference, a proposed permittivity-based terrain instrument, a gamma densitometer design with Mars mission heritage, and a laboratory radio-frequency prototype that measures mass rather than density. They are not directly comparable and should not be read as a ranking.

examples.name: Apollo 16 Lunar Self-Recording Penetrometer
examples.type: Flown lunar penetrometer; density and porosity are inferred, not measured directly
examples.cone_configuration: Sources disagree. The Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report lists two cones (base areas 1.29 and 3.22 cm2); the PDS instrument description lists three cones (1.29, 3.22 and 6.45 cm2). Both state a 30 degree apex angle.
examples.measurement_principle: Penetration force deflects a calibrated coil spring, which rotates a recording drum in proportion to force.
examples.reported_density_range_g_cm3: approx. 1.0 to 2.0 (from search-result text of the report; not confirmed on the page read)
examples.reported_mean_porosity_percent: 43.3 at earlier landing sites; approx. 46-47 on slopes (search-result text; not confirmed on the page read)
examples.qualification: Flown instrument. Mass figure is for the whole instrument, not a cone alone.

examples.name: Terrain Testing Instrument (TTI), Chang'e 8
examples.type: Proposed lunar terrain instrument; not flown
examples.flight_status: Proposed and in development. Selected payload on the JINNAH-1 rover for a 2029 launch, per the abstract. Structural model delivered; electrical model due summer 2026.
examples.mass_note: About 1.5 kg total, with electronics housed inside the rover
examples.sensor_configuration: Linear-mechanism cone penetrometer, rotating shear vane, and integrated permittivity sensor
examples.qualification: Figures come from a single conference abstract and were not cross-checked with the mission.

examples.name: Gamma-ray densitometer (DEN) of the HP3 package
examples.type: Subsurface gamma densitometer design; 2006 breadboard; HP3 flown on NASA InSight (Mars)
examples.flight_status: The HP3 package flew on InSight. DEN's density results were not confirmed in this review.
examples.source: Caesium-137 gamma source with tungsten shielding rod
examples.measurement_principle: Density determined at regular intervals during penetration from the gamma-ray spectrum, which depends on Compton scattering in the surrounding material
examples.calibration: Test materials and a Monte Carlo model (2006 breadboard)
examples.qualification: The 2006 abstract PDF did not yield readable text in the fetch; details are from search-result summaries.

examples.name: Radio-frequency microstrip sensor for excavator regolith mass (laboratory prototype)
examples.type: Laboratory prototype; estimates regolith mass in a scoop, not bulk density
examples.flight_status: Laboratory only. Rotary clamshell excavator engineering model rated TRL 6; sample sensor and vibration motor at lower TRL.
examples.line: 50 ohm open-ended microstrip on RF35 laminate (permittivity 3.5)

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a regolith density sensor. Published external dimensions were not found for the TTI, the DEN subsystem or the RF prototype. The Apollo penetrometer's bearing plate measured 2.54 x 12.7 cm; its overall housing dimensions were not stated in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Apollo 16 penetrometer: 2.3 kg (PDS). TTI: about 1.5 kg total (abstract, proposed). DEN subsystem mass not found. RF prototype mass not applicable (laboratory setup).
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for any of the four examples. The Apollo 16 instrument's power and the DEN's power were not found.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A regolith density sensor must operate in the lunar surface environment, with large temperature variations, vacuum, radiation and dust. Methods that rely on electromagnetic properties (permittivity and radio-frequency reflection) are sensitive to the state of the soil, and the RF study did not control or monitor temperature or humidity, assuming 20–25 °C and 30–60% relative humidity [6]. The TTI abstract links its permittivity measurement to both density and ice content [5], so interpretation must account for both. A gamma-source densitometer would bring radiological licensing, handling and safety requirements that depend on national and mission rules; these requirements were not specified in the sources reviewed. Penetration-based methods require a stable reference and good contact with the soil, and their results depend on the mechanical state of the regolith. Measurement location matters: density varies with depth, and surface compaction can differ from the material a few tens of centimetres below.
article.limitations: The sensor class has no flight-proven member dedicated to regolith density in the sources reviewed. The Apollo penetrometer infers density and porosity indirectly rather than measuring them. The TTI is proposed. The DEN design is a 2006 breadboard whose lunar relevance is through its Mars heritage, and whose flight results were not confirmed. The RF prototype estimates mass in a simulant rather than density in real regolith. Remote density estimates from radar depend on assumed calibrations and cover depth ranges that differ from in-situ sensors [4]. Core-based values depend on sample disturbance and sampling depth [3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A regolith density sensor would be a surface or shallow-subsurface instrument carried on a lander or rover. Its deployment mechanism, power and data interfaces depend on the carrier, which has not been identified for any in-development example.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor and any penetration mechanism into the lander or rover payload envelope on Earth.
Launch and transfer to the Moon under the carrier's requirements.
Land and deliver the sensor to the surface, with mounting constrained by landing loads and thermal conditions.
Deploy by a dedicated penetration mechanism (the TTI uses a linear mechanism) or by astronaut or robotic handling (the Apollo 16 penetrometer was operated during an EVA).
Connect power and data; interfaces are not specified for the examples and the TTI's electronics sit inside its rover.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Dedicated linear-mechanism penetration (TTI, about 5 cm depth) or astronaut-operated penetration (Apollo 16 penetrometer, maximum 76 cm depth).
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 16 Lunar Self-Recording Penetrometer (eleven tests during the second EVA); HP3 package with DEN on InSight (Mars), which is not a lunar deployment.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander or rover has been verified. The JINNAH-1 rover is the only named carrier in the sources reviewed for the TTI, and its compatibility with any lander was not checked.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 penetrometer was one of the early in-situ tools used to characterise the mechanical properties of lunar soil, and its test campaign during the second EVA provided penetration data at two stations [2]. Apollo core-tube and drill-core samples provided laboratory density measurements that remain key reference values [3]. Radar-based estimates from Chang'e-3 extended the picture to greater depth [4]. The HP3 package on InSight, which carried the DEN design, took a subsurface density-related instrument concept to Mars, although DEN's density results are not confirmed here [7][8]. A 2026 review abstract notes that no dedicated instrument has yet been flown on modern landing and roving missions to measure regolith physical properties [5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Flight status.** No dedicated regolith density sensor was identified as flown on a lunar mission. The TTI is proposed; the RF sensor is a laboratory prototype; the DEN design is a breadboard with Mars heritage whose results were not confirmed; the Apollo penetrometer flew but measures resistance, not density.
- **Numerical values from search summaries.** The Apollo 16 density range (1.0–2.0 g/cm³), porosity values (43.3% and 46–47%) and the count of eleven penetrometer tests were taken from search-result text of the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report [2]. The page that was read did not contain a numerical density range, and the full tables were not checked.
- **Conflicting cone configuration.** The Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report describes two cones [2], while the PDS instrument description lists three cones including a 6.45 cm² cone [1]. This article does not resolve the conflict.
- **Core-based density values.** Search summaries give an Apollo-era surface bulk density of about 1.3 g/cm³ rising to about 1.92 g/cm³ at depth, with porosities of about 58% at the surface and 38% at depth [3]. These were not verified against the full paper, and the paper's title and authorship were not confirmed.
- **Radar-based density range.** The Chang'e-3 radar study is reported in search-result text as giving density rising from about 0.85 g/cm³ at the surface to about 2.25 g/cm³ at 5 m [4]. This is a remote estimate and was not verified in full.
- **DEN specifications.** The DEN description comes from a 2006 conference abstract [7] whose PDF did not yield readable text in the fetch, so details are taken from search-result summaries. A search summary also suggests the InSight mole reached about 40 cm rather than its planned depth; this was not verified.
- **TTI schedule and mass.** The mass, depth and launch date come from a single conference abstract [5] and were not cross-checked with the mission.
- **Not established.** Mass and power of a standalone density sensor, radiological requirements for a gamma source, dedicated lunar density instrument heritage, and lander compatibility were not found or verified.
- **Images.** No images were verified for this draft, so none are included.
